practiceRuns.feedback: A lucky correct guess does not supply adequate grounds. Calling it knowledge would skip the problem the example is designed to expose.
The belief is true, but the stated case supplies no evidence justifying it. Correctness alone does not establish knowledge.
The belief is true, not false. Its missing ingredient in the stated case is adequate evidence.
The accepted time is false. The hidden fault can leave the person with apparently reasonable grounds, so falsity does not by itself show that all justification is absent.
The person still accepts the clock’s time. Belief is present; truth is missing.
A reasonable reliance on a normally reliable clock may be fallibly justified despite an undetected fault. The case does not establish that all justification is missing.
The proposition can be true at the moment of coincidence. The issue is whether the three proposed conditions suffice for knowledge.
The case challenges the sufficiency of justified true belief. On a plausible reading, all three conditions hold while the truth depends problematically on luck.
The person does believe the displayed time. Belief and truth are not what the example calls into question.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid implication into a valid proof. The derivation has not established the conclusion.
One successful instance cannot establish the reversed implication universally. Nine is a counterexample to odd implying prime.
Neither follows through that argument. The conclusion may be true and supported by another proof, but this derivation has not established it.
